_comment: The auto-marked half of E7's assessment. Twenty questions across two
sections, plus the written answer described in content/rubrics/e7.json.
Open book, on purpose. 10b: 'Notes and the lessons are allowed. Questions
ask you to apply a method, not recall a fact.' So none of these can be
answered by finding a sentence — every one puts the learner in a situation
and asks what they would do. Having E7 open in another tab is no help if you
did not understand it, which is the property a closed-book test of
These are NOT the lesson quizzes. A learner who memorised every lesson quiz
would still have to think here, and the stems are deliberately unlike the
quiz stems so that the Sky assessment guard treats them as distinct.
They are indexed by scripts/build-sky-index.mjs into the assessment guard,
so the site assistant refuses to answer them. That matters more here than
for a lesson quiz: a lesson quiz getting spoiled costs a learner some
practice, and this getting spoiled costs a certificate its meaning.

items.q: Your team's slide deck says a competitor grew 40% last year. The figure came from a colleague who read it somewhere. The deck goes to the board tomorrow. What does the first of the three standing questions tell you to do?
options: Check it, because every number in a board deck must be verified
Ask whether anything changes if the number is wrong, and check only if something does
Remove the number, since its source is unknown
items.explain: Question one is the volume control: does this matter if it is wrong? A board deck usually means yes — but the habit is to ask first, not to check reflexively. Checking everything is how people stop checking anything.

items.q: Which of these claims most needs checking before you repeat it?
options: A friend says the new café on the corner opens at eight
A post says a medicine you are about to give your child interacts badly with another
A colleague says the meeting room is on the third floor
items.explain: Triage is about consequence, not confidence. The first two are self-correcting within minutes at trivial cost; the third could harm someone before you find out it was wrong.

items.q: You notice you are about to check a statistic only because it contradicts what you already believe. What does that tell you?
options: That your instinct is working — contradictory claims are more often wrong
That you should also check the last claim you accepted because it agreed with you
That you should check it more carefully than usual
items.explain: The asymmetry is the signal. If disagreement is what triggers scrutiny, then everything you agreed with went through unchecked — and that is where your errors are accumulating, unnoticed.

items.q: An assistant gives you a fluent, well-organised, confidently written summary of a report. What have you learned about whether the summary is accurate?
options: Nothing — fluency and accuracy are produced by different things
That it is probably accurate, since errors usually show as hedging
That it is accurate on the main points but may be wrong on details
items.explain: Fluency is what the system optimises for. Accuracy is not, and the two come apart without any visible signal — which is why a confident wrong answer looks exactly like a confident right one.

items.q: You have twenty claims in a document and forty minutes. What is the best use of the time?
options: Check every claim briefly so nothing is unexamined
Check the two or three that the argument actually rests on, properly
Check the ones you are least sure about
items.explain: A shallow pass over twenty claims verifies nothing and feels like diligence. Load-bearing claims get real checks; decorative ones can be dropped instead.

items.q: A message from your manager's address asks you to urgently move a payment to a new account. Which feature of it should decide your response?
options: Whether the writing style matches how they usually write
That it asks for money or access, regardless of how convincing it is
Whether the email address is exactly right
items.explain: Style and address are both cheap to forge, so neither can carry the decision. The category of the request is what triggers out-of-band confirmation — you verify by a channel you chose, not one they supplied.

items.q: Which situation most reliably produces a verification failure?
options: A complicated claim you do not have expertise in
A deadline, plus a claim that says what you were hoping it would say
A source you have never heard of
items.explain: Unfamiliar sources and hard claims make you cautious. Pressure plus a welcome answer removes the impulse to check at exactly the moment checking matters, which is why the habit has to be small enough to run anyway.

items.q: You are told a claim came from 'a government report'. What is the least useful next step?
options: Asking which report, from which department, and when
Searching for other articles that mention the same figure
Finding the report and reading the relevant sentence
items.explain: Other articles repeating a figure are not independent confirmation — they usually share one origin. Ten restatements of one unchecked claim is still one unchecked claim.

items.q: When is it correct to decide not to check something at all?
options: When the source is one you have trusted before
When nothing you do would change if the claim turned out to be false
When checking would take longer than the task is worth
items.explain: You are allowed to not check things, and the criterion is consequence rather than convenience or familiarity. Cost is a real constraint, but it is not what makes a claim safe to skip.

items.q: A striking claim spreads quickly and makes you feel strongly. What does the strength of that reaction suggest about the claim's origin?
options: Nothing about its truth, but it is evidence the claim was selected for reaction
That it is likely false, since true claims are usually boring
That it is probably true, since fabrications are rarely this specific
items.explain: Whatever produces a strong reaction spreads further, so the things that reach you are filtered for reaction rather than accuracy. That says nothing about truth and a great deal about why this one arrived.

items.q: You open a cited source and the sentence it supposedly supports is not there — but a similar sentence is, about a different country. What is the correct conclusion?
options: The claim is supported, since the mechanism is likely the same elsewhere
The citation does not support the claim, and repeating it would be a misuse of the source
The claim is false
items.explain: The claim may still be true — but this source does not establish it, and that is the finding. Treating a near-match as support is how a figure about one place ends up cited for another.

items.q: An assistant produces a citation with a plausible author, journal and year. You cannot find the paper. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The paper exists but is not indexed where you searched
The citation was assembled from the shape of real citations and does not refer to anything
The paper has been retracted
items.explain: A citation is a pattern like any other, and a system that produces plausible text produces plausible citations. The rule that follows is absolute: never repeat a citation you have not opened.

items.q: You ask an assistant whether its previous answer was correct and it says yes. What has that established?
options: Nothing — the same system is not an independent check on itself
That the answer is likely correct, since it had a chance to reconsider
That the answer is internally consistent
items.explain: 'Are you sure?' is not a check. Confirmation from the same source is one source twice, and the agreement is produced by the same process that produced the original answer.

items.q: Two reputable sources give different figures for the same quantity. What should you look at first?
options: Which source is more recent
Whether they are measuring the same thing over the same period and population
Which source is generally more reliable
items.explain: Most apparent disagreements are definitional. Before deciding who is wrong, establish whether they are answering the same question — often neither is wrong and the comparison was never valid.

items.q: You have two minutes to check a claim. What gets you furthest?
options: Reading three articles about it
Finding who originally said it and reading that sentence in place
Asking an assistant to verify it
items.explain: Two minutes is enough to reach an origin, and reaching the origin is the whole method. Reading around a claim can be done indefinitely without ever testing it.

items.q: A source is a well-designed site with citations, an about page and an editorial policy. How much does that tell you?
options: A great deal — those signals are expensive to produce
Little on its own, since all of it is cheap to imitate and none of it is a check on the content
Enough to treat it as reliable for uncontroversial claims
items.explain: Every one of those signals is presentation. What matters is whether the claims resolve to sources that say what they are said to say — which you find by following one, not by admiring the layout.

items.q: You verified a figure last year and it is still being quoted. What is the risk in repeating it now?
options: None — a verified figure stays verified
The figure may be accurate for its period and misleading as a description of today
The original source may have been withdrawn
items.explain: Verification is anchored to a date, which is why anything published with a figure should carry when it was checked. A correct 2025 number presented as current is a false claim made out of true material.

items.q: Which statement would you most trust from a colleague?
options: "It's 12% — I checked the ONS release, though I have not confirmed it uses our definition"
"It's around 12%, but don't quote me on that"
items.explain: The first claims less and is worth more: it tells you exactly what was established, what was not, and where it might fail. Vagueness is not humility — it gives the reader nothing to weigh.

items.q: You find that a claim you published last month was wrong. What is the best response?
options: Quietly correct it, since drawing attention to it spreads the error further
Correct it visibly and dated, so anyone who relied on it can see what changed
Leave it and correct it in the next piece
items.explain: The people who need the correction are the ones who already took the claim away with them, and a silent edit reaches none of them. A dated correction is also what makes the rest of your record worth trusting.

items.q: After running all three standing questions you are less certain than you were before. What has happened?
options: You checked badly — good verification increases confidence
The method worked: your confidence has moved towards what the evidence supports
The claim is probably false
items.explain: Verification calibrates rather than reassures. Ending up less sure, and able to say exactly why, is a better position than the confidence you started with — and it is the point of the whole module.
